Demand to restore pensionary benefits to RBI Employees 
 SHRI K. CHANDRAN PILLAI (Kerala):  Sir, I rise to draw the attention of the House and also 
of the Government to the countrywide strike by almost the entire workforce, 25,000 employees 
and officers, of the country’s central bank, the Re serve Bank of India, which is going to take 
place tomorrow on 20th February 2009. 
 The strike has been forced upon them by  the Government by imposing unilateral and 
arrogant decision to curtail the pension bene fits of the RBI employees decided by the RBI 
Management Board and implemented since 2003. In 2003, the RBI Board decided to update the 
pension payment of the retired employees following the pay revision of the regular employees. In 
2008, the Government forced the RBI management to withdraw such updated pension benefits 
for the employees and officers revised in 2003 following the regular pay revision of the 
employees. This resulted in reduction of pension by Rs. 1,000 to Rs. 6,000 for around 4,000 
retired employees; and such forcible withdrawal of the revision of pension benefits is going to 
adversely affect the pension rights of the existing employees as well. 
 It is ridiculous that while the Central Pay Commission allowed upward revision of pension 
benefits for the retirees in Government serv ices, how could the Government deny similar 
provision for pension-revision for the RBI employees, even when RBI management has managed 
the same from its own resources without any budgetary support? I demand that the Government 
must review its unjust and irrational decision in this regard forthwith in consultation with the 
employees and officers’ association of RBI to avoid aggravation of industrial unrest in RBI.

Concern over the matter of dumping of Butter oil by European countries in India 
 SHRI NARESH GUJRAL (Punjab): Sir, I would lik e to draw the attention of the House to the 
fact that the India dairy industry is facing a very serious crisis which is directly impacting our poor 
farmers. 
 The European countries and New Zealand are dumping butter oil which is the raw material 
for making ghee in our country. They are able to do so thank s to the generous subsidies that 
they receive from their respective Governme nts. The U.S. is also contemplating the 
reintroduction of Dairy Export Incentive Programme which would further accentuate the problem. 
 Based on the current price of raw milk being pa id to the Indian farmer, milk fat (butter or 
ghee) is being sold at around Rs. 175 per kg. in the country. However, the imported butter oil 
and animal milk fat lands in India at approximately Rs. 130/- per kg., including freight and duty at 
46 per cent. This is resulting in depressing th e demand as well as the price for raw milk being 
produced by our farmers.  
 Sir, we are all aware that thanks to the glob al financial meltdown, Indian exports are hurting 
while imports are surging resulting in a huge trade deficit for the country. It is imperative to curtail 
all unnecessary imports. 
 Hence, I would urge upon the Government to  protect the poor Indian farmers and ensure 
that our country does not become a dumping grou nd for heavily subsidized imported butter oil 
and animal milk fat. The Government must incr ease the import duty to, at least, 100 per cent 
with immediate effect. At the same time, it must be withdraw the facility of 5 per cent import duty 
on skimmed milk power which was offered to cooperatives in April, 2008, with the intention to 
contain the high inflation rate at that time.

The Central Industries Security Force (Amendment) Bill, 2008 
 THE MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (SHRI P. CHIDAMBARAM): Sir, I beg to move: 
That the Bill further to amend the Central Indust rial Security Force Act, 1968, be taken into 
consideration. 
 Sir, this is a Bill to amend the Central Indust rial Security Force Act to enable the CISF to 
extend security cover to establishments in the private sector, as well as, in the joint sector. 

 314
There are a number of establishmen ts in the joint sector, as well as, in the private sector which 
are important both to the economy and to the s ecurity of the country. Some examples are oil 
installations, refineries, coal mi nes, ports, etc., and, therefore, we think that the times demand 
that the CISF be, probably, extended to these establishments also. That is the main purpose of 
this amendment. The CISF is one of our best-trained and best-equipped forces today. It has a 
strength of 1,12,534 officers and men. It is de ployed in 280 establishments. We have permitted 
further raising of the CISF to 1,45,000. We think, with the demands that are coming in, the 
strength of this Force can be raised over a period of time and deployed. The CISF, of course, will 
continue to provide security to the public sector  establishments and many more will be covered. 
There will be no, I will repeat there will be no, question of reducing the CISF cover to the public 
sector. The first claim to the CISF will be of the Government and the public sector. As the Force 
is raised and its strength increases, we will re spond to requests from the joint sector and the

 SHRI S. S. AHLUWALIA: Sir, before we adjourned for lunch I was speaking on CISF Bill. 
Sir, I was making a point that CISF should not be used as a watch and ward. If you make a two-
tier system in security, wherever you are prov iding security, you train their watch and ward 
people, you train their security people as per the requirements of CISF and make a strategic unit, 
provide them only a strategic team which can be  used as a combating force with any terrorist 
attack or which will be dealing with the terrorist attacks only and they should be deputed on the 
strategic points. Otherwise, what will happen is, once you give the duty of CISF to the watch 
and ward there will be lot of hassles or a lot of problems. Let the other problems be dealt with by 
the private companies themselves and their people  should be trained by CISF and for that you 
must charge them, you must take money from th em and you give a well trained combating unit 
so that they can protect the establishment from  any terrorist attack. Sir, for that, women and 
men, both should be trained because in a compan y like Infosys you will find that there are plenty 
of women IT engineers who are working and when  you are facing this, the terrorist may, the 
Fidayeen may come in the shape of a lady suicide bomber or suicide attack team. To deal with 
them women also are needed. I believe that ther e are enough women in the CISF so that they 
can get training. Sir, for training and for their skilled development you must have sophisticated 
weapons also. I do not know, today we are having  maximum SLRs or automatic rifles or we are 
having in some places AK-47 or so. The terrorists  are using the latest technology and the latest 
weapons. To combat with them we should have that weapon also. When we are deputing these 
people to combat terrorists, they must be provid ed with that type of weapons so that they can 
combat efficiently. Sir, modern communication is required. We have seen that we do not have 
the modern communication facilities. We have lear nt from 26/11. They were using Blackberries. 
They were using satellite phones. They were using a plenty of other things. Recently, a new virus 
has attacked the software and has paralysed the whole communication system in Tajikistan. We 
should learn from all these thin gs and virus-proof, foolproof firewall software should be made 
available for communications system in the CISF.
